title: Trump cites ten-year low in gas prices; earlier figures show similar lows
text: Gas prices are expected to rise sharply this year, but Donald Trump believes that a ten-year low on a single day is something for which he should receive credit. On July 4th, gas prices fell to an average of $2.23 a gallon, the lowest level on Independence Day in ten years. Trump commented on the figure on Twitter on July 4, 2017: "Gas prices are the lowest in the U.S. in over ten years! I would like to see them go even lower." The year 2017 is only half over, and one day does not equal one year. Presidents do not control gas prices. Conservatives point this out when gas prices fall during a Democratic presidency or rise during a Republican presidency, a position they apply inconsistently. When gas prices are low during a Republican presidency, conservatives set that knowledge aside and credit the president. That is the case now. Trump had no role in current gas prices. The market has been flooded with oversupply from OPEC, which has driven the price of gasoline down over the last couple of years. In 2015, the national average price of gas fell to $2.35, from $3.37 in 2014. On Independence Day last year, the price of gas was $2.26 per gallon, three cents more than the low Trump cited the previous day. Conservatives did not give President Obama credit for that price. They also did not credit Obama for the lower national average of $2.20 per gallon in November 2016. Oversupply is the reason gas is cheaper now. Once that supply is used up, the price of gas will rise again, and Trump has no means of preventing it.

title: Chile's economic team walks out – a crushing blow to Bachelet's coalition!
text: Chilean President Michelle Bachelet's top economic officials quit on Thursday after a major mining project was scrapped. The timing could hardly be worse: her center-left coalition is left weakened before November elections. Finance Minister Rodrigo Valdes did not hold back at a news conference. Some members of Bachelet's government, he said, had simply not shared his sense of urgency to spur growth and attract investment to the world's top copper producer. "I wasn't able to make everybody share this conviction," Valdes said, pointing to the need for discipline and clear rules for the private sector. Valdes, who held the job for two years, had slammed the government's decision last week to reject a $2.5 billion copper and iron project owned by Andes Iron on environmental grounds. So had Economy Minister Luis Felipe Cespedes and Finance Undersecretary Alejandro Micco. Both of them are gone too. Why did Cespedes quit? Talking with reporters, he would not say. Micco's office declined to comment on his reasons. The project, known as Dominga, had become a symbol in recent months of the growing difficulties of doing business in what remains one of Latin America's most open economies. And it ripped open the philosophical rifts inside the government. Bachelet said Valdes will be replaced by Nicolas Eyzaguirre, an economist in charge of legislative affairs for the president, while Cespedes will be replaced by Jorge Rodriguez, president of Banco del Estado de Chile. Her defense? "I don't think development is something to be done with your back to the people, where only the numbers matter and not what's happening to families," said Bachelet. Some saw the shakeup as a heavy blow to the center-left and its presidential candidate Alejandro Guillier, who is generally supportive of Bachelet, and a gift to conservative frontrunner Sebastian Pinera.

title: Game on! Final New Zealand count hands Labour fresh firepower in coalition fight
text: The race is tightening! A possible Labour-Green coalition clawed back ground on the ruling National Party in New Zealand's final election tally, boosting their hand ahead of crunch talks on Sunday with the small nationalist party that holds the balance of power. The final results of the Sept. 23 election, released on Saturday, showed National with 56 seats and Labour and the Greens together on 54. Neither side can get there alone. Both are now at the mercy of New Zealand First's nine seats to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority in parliament under New Zealand's proportional representation system. National lost two seats to the Labour-Green bloc compared with the preliminary results. Labour leader Jacinda Ardern said it buoyed their position at the negotiating table. "We will continue our negotiations in earnest with potential support parties beginning this weekend," Ardern told reporters in Auckland. "This now means that we have a strengthened mandate to negotiate and form a durable, stable coalition government." And what a rise it has been. Ardern, 37, took over the Labour leadership barely two months before the election and was quickly compared with youthful, cosmopolitan leaders like Canada's Justin Trudeau and France's Emmanuel Macron. She has almost single-handedly hauled Labour to within reach of government. So who will kingmaker New Zealand First choose? In an emailed statement, the party said it would hold discussions on Sunday with the National Party at midday and with the Labour Party in the afternoon. New Zealand First leader Winston Peters told local media that "knowing the facts puts us in a better position to make judgements". Peters has said he will decide which party to back only after the final tally and after the results become official on Oct. 12. The suspense continues!

title: Democrats pounce! Trump's allies feel the heat over his attack on a judge
text: Democrats smelled blood. On Monday, Democratic leaders across the nation set out to make Republican officials and candidates pay a political price for still backing Donald J. Trump after his explosive remarks questioning the objectivity of judges with Mexican or Muslim backgrounds. The attacks came from everywhere at once: congressional offices and the Senate floor, state capitols and sidewalk protests. In an unusually coordinated barrage, Democrats tore into Mr. Trump as racist and demanded that Republicans either stand behind his comments or condemn him, and even rescind their endorsements of his candidacy. And who handed them the ammunition? Mr. Trump himself. In an extraordinary conference call with allies on Monday, he urged them to defend his criticisms of a federal judge's Mexican heritage, then scolded his own campaign staff for having suggested otherwise. His stubbornness, and his rebuke of his own aides, left Republicans feeling powerless. They said they increasingly saw no way to influence Mr. Trump's behavior or to convince him that his actions could damage the party in competitive House, Senate and governor's races. Reince Priebus, the chairman of the Republican National Committee, has discussed with Mr. Trump his attacks on Judge Gonzalo P. Curiel of Federal District Court, who is overseeing a suit against Trump University, according to a Republican briefed on the talks. But Mr. Priebus has had similar conversations with Mr. Trump for months, to little avail. Other senior Republicans were confused about whether it was even worth approaching any of Mr. Trump's aides about staging an intervention. Republican candidates in tough races this fall were left to fend for themselves! Senator Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire called on Mr. Trump to retract his comments about Judge Curiel, calling them "offensive and wrong." The other candidates? They kept their heads down.

title: "Not winning": Mattis delivers grim Afghanistan verdict to Congress
text: A stunning admission. The United States is "not winning" the war against Taliban insurgents in Afghanistan, Defense Secretary Jim Mattis told Congress on Tuesday. He promised to brief lawmakers by mid-July on a new war strategy that is widely expected to call for thousands more U.S. troops. Thousands more! The remarks were a blunt reminder of the gloom hanging over U.S. military assessments of the war between the U.S.-backed Afghan government and the Islamist militant group, a war U.S. commanders classify as a "stalemate" despite almost 16 years of fighting. “We are not winning in Afghanistan right now. And we will correct this as soon as possible,” Mattis said in testimony to the Senate Armed Services Committee. Mattis admitted he believed the Taliban were "surging" right now, something he said he intended to address. But will more troops even help? Some U.S. officials doubted it, arguing that any politically palatable number would not be enough to turn the tide, let alone create stability and security. The toll is staggering. More than 2,300 Americans have been killed and more than 17,000 wounded since the war began in 2001. The U.S. military assessed that the Afghan government controlled or influenced just 59.7 percent of Afghanistan's 407 districts as of Feb. 20, a drop of nearly 11 percentage points from the same time in 2016, according to data released by the U.S. Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction. Last month a truck bomb in Kabul killed more than 150 people, the deadliest attack in the Afghan capital since the Taliban were ousted in 2001 by a NATO-led coalition after ruling the country for five years. And on Saturday, three U.S. soldiers were killed when an Afghan soldier opened fire on them in eastern Afghanistan.

title: North Carolina drug tested welfare recipients; results show low rate of drug use
text: The results run counter to Republican expectations, and they give taxpayers reason to be angry. Republicans were certain that welfare recipients use drugs, and they passed a bill requiring applicants to take a drug test in order to receive government aid, with the aim of humiliating poor people. The governor vetoed the legislation, but Republicans, intent on targeting poor people, overrode the veto. Testing took some time because more than 7,600 people needed to be screened. The results have now been released, and the numbers do not support the Republican position. Although Republicans were convinced enough that welfare recipients were drug users to spend taxpayer money on a program intended to prove it, the program produced the opposite result. Only 21 of the people tested were positive for drug use. That is 0.3 percent of those tested, well below the national average of 8 percent. Elected officials could themselves be required to take a mandatory drug test to remain in office.

title: One rumor, then fire and death: terror grips a tense Kenyan slum
text: It all began with a single rumor: the Mungiki, a feared Kikuyu tribal militia, had slipped into Nairobi's Kawangware slum. Within minutes, local men already inflamed by Kenya's bitterly divisive election had seized machetes and sticks to defend their turf. By the end of Friday night's clash, a man had been beaten to death and rows of shops and homes were in flames. It was a chilling glimpse of how fast ethnic violence can explode in the Kenyan capital's volatile slums. Almost all of the 50 deaths since August's presidential vote have come in clashes between protesters and police. But Kenyans fear something far worse. Could the months of political strife, made worse by the courts annulling the August vote, eat away at deep tribal divisions and unleash a wave of inter-ethnic bloodshed? It has happened before: after a disputed 2007 vote, 1,200 people were killed. The Kawangware fighting was triggered by rumors that the Kikuyu, the tribe of President Uhuru Kenyatta, had brought in Mungiki members to protect them from opposition supporters. On Friday, a witness saw a group of men armed with machetes, known locally as pangas, on the streets of Kawangware. Who were they? Nobody could say for sure, though several residents said they were Mungiki, brought in after opposition loyalists burned down a prominent Kikuyu-owned business the night before. The Mungiki, notorious for castrating and beheading victims, were blamed for hundreds of deaths in the 2007 clashes. Their relative quiet since then has done nothing to soften that terrifying reputation. "They were more than a hundred, and they were carrying all new pangas," said Vitalis Aloyi, a Kawangware resident. Another man said residents had to act to defend themselves. "We had to teach them not to bring Mungiki here."

title: Kurdish giant Jalal Talabani dies – just days after the explosive independence vote
text: A towering figure is gone. Iraqi Kurdish leader and former Iraqi president Jalal Talabani died on Tuesday at age 83, Iraqi state TV said. His death came just a week after Iraq's autonomous Kurdish region held its referendum on independence. Talabani, a veteran leader of the Kurdish struggle for self-determination, stepped down as president in 2014 after a long period of treatment following a stroke in 2012. He died in Germany, according to Erbil-based Rudaw TV, which had reported earlier in the day that his health had worsened. He often went to Germany for medical treatment. And the timing? His wife and partner in political struggle, Hero, and his Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) party gave only lukewarm support to the Sept. 25 referendum, which delivered an overwhelming yes to secession from Iraq. Unlike Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) leader Massoud Barzani of the rival Kurdish Democratic Party (KDP), the PUK has traditionally had good ties with Iran and the Iranian-backed Shi'ite groups that effectively rule in Baghdad. The Baghdad government, Iran and Turkey all fiercely opposed the referendum. Talabani was born in 1933 near Erbil, now the seat of the autonomous KRG in northern Iraq. He lived in Sulaimaniya, a stronghold of his PUK, the main rival of Barzani's KDP. He made history as the first non-Arab president of Iraq, elected in 2005, two years after the U.S.-led invasion that toppled dictator Saddam Hussein, a Sunni Arab. Fuad Masoum, a Kurd from the PUK, replaced Talabani in the Iraqi presidency, a largely ceremonial post in the system set up after Saddam's overthrow, which concentrates power in the hands of the prime minister, now Haider al-Abadi, an Arab Shi'ite Muslim. One of Talabani's sons, Qubad, is the current deputy prime minister of the autonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq.

title: Downpours, gales and a veil blown into the sky! 6 tips to save your rain-soaked wedding
text: Foul weather nearly wrecked it. Instead, it gave Tiffany Mallory's wedding to Jerrell Moore its most dramatic moment. “It had been pouring, and then it stopped raining but turned cold and windy right as we started the ceremony,” said Mrs. Mallory Moore, who was married April 2 in front of 140 guests on the back lawn of the Mint Museum in Charlotte, N.C. As she battled through the squall to meet her groom at the altar, a gust ripped her veil off and sent it into the sky! “It went flying, right off my head,” she said. “But I’m over six feet tall, so people thought it looked very glamorous.” After a soaking April and May on the East Coast, plenty of couples learned the hard way that a perfect (or at least nearly perfect) wedding does not need perfect weather. “Did my guests get wet? title: Case thrown out! Rick Perry finally escapes abuse-of-power indictment
text: It's over. On Wednesday the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals threw out an abuse of power indictment against Rick Perry, ending a case that weighed down the former Texas governor's failed bid for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination. Perry, who ran for the nomination in 2012 and 2016, had faced a first-degree felony charge in state courts that could have carried up to 99 years in prison. His offense? A funding veto he made in 2013, seen as an attempt to force a Texas county district attorney to resign. “When the only act that is being prosecuted is a veto, then the prosecution itself violates separation of powers,” the court said. The longest serving governor in Texas history, Perry, 65, was indicted on the two charges in August 2014 by a grand jury in Travis County, a Democratic stronghold in the heavily Republican state. Perry came out swinging. “The court’s decision today proves that this indictment was nothing less than a baseless political attack,” Perry told a news conference. “I have always known that the actions that I took were not only lawful and legal - they were right.” He first threatened and then vetoed $7.5 million for an integrity unit in the Travis County District Attorney's office. Many said Perry played hardball politics to drive out county District Attorney Rosemary Lehmberg, a Democrat, after she pleaded guilty to drunken driving. In July 2015, a Texas state appeals court tossed a lesser charge against Perry for coercion of a public official, leaving only the abuse-of-power charge. Lawyers for Perry, whose term ended at the start of 2015, have argued the governor was acting within his powers when he cut the funding. But a prosecutor in the case said Perry acted unlawfully to pressure Lehmberg by threatening the funding cut.

McCollum (20.8) – a quick team in a loose image of the Golden State Warriors, led by Stephen Curry (30.1 points per game) and Klay Thompson (22.1)! The series between two of the most thrilling backcourts around began Sunday WITHOUT Curry, out indefinitely with a knee sprain! And you won't believe what happened: Thompson ran RIGHT OVER Lillard and McCollum in Game 1! He scored early and often as the Warriors raced to a quick lead and, in the end, a win at Oracle Arena! For much of the first quarter, Lillard and McCollum were just as effective as Curry – who was sitting on the bench in a blazer – as they combined to MISS their first seven shots! Thompson, guarding Lillard, dropped 12 of his 37 points in the first six minutes as the Warriors took the lead! “Not many guys in the league could chase Damian Lillard around for 37 minutes and score 37 points, too,” Golden State Coach Steve Kerr said. “Klay is a tremendous player.” When Lillard FINALLY scored, and was fouled, on a driving layup with about 30 seconds left in the first quarter, the Blazers were STILL behind – and Thompson fired right back!

title: Collusion?! All 100 senators reached out to the Russian government this week
text: Attorney General Jeff Sessions landed in a firestorm this week because he answered a question about the Trump campaign's contacts with the Russian government without mentioning his own contacts as a United States Senator. The media, the Democrats and even some Republicans all assumed that even routine contact with the Russian government carries the stench of collusion. Not since the McCarthy era has suspicion run this high. But if Sessions should resign, shouldn't the entire Senate quit too? Here's why. On Monday, two days before the Washington Post broke the supposedly scandalous story that Sessions had met the Russian ambassador twice in the course of his duties, every single United States Senator had formal contact with the Russian government. And not with some functionary, either: they contacted Russian President Vladimir Putin himself! Worse (apparently) still, they made the first move. The contact was a letter, signed by the entire Senate, urging Putin to release a valuable library of Jewish religious texts that was seized by earlier Russian regimes and has been the subject of a legal and diplomatic dispute in recent decades. Senator Orrin Hatch added the final signature to the 2017 Senate letter regarding Chabad and proudly tweeted his support for the effort: "For the last year, Hatch has led his colleagues in an effort to recover the texts, including a letter signed by all 100 Senators." None of that means Sessions should have misled Congress. But the point, once again, is that he did not.

title: Trump accuses American soldiers of stealing millions of dollars of aid money in Iraq
text: Since the start of Trump's unlikely political career, it has been clear that his contempt for American soldiers is close to pathological. He occasionally praises the troops when pressed, though reluctantly. More often, the Republican nominee, who deferred his own military service in Vietnam a number of times, shows open disgust for them. He accused John McCain of being a loser because he was captured and tortured by the North Vietnamese, while Trump did not serve in the war. More recently he used the military as a reason to avoid an uncomfortable primary debate, and then withheld the money he raised for veterans until this was made public. Trump has now accused unnamed Iraq War veterans of stealing millions of dollars from the U.S. government that were meant to help rebuild the country after the war. The remark is likely to appear in Hillary Clinton's next campaign advertisement. Such a theft would be a serious crime. Trump made the accusation casually. The Republican presidential nominee said: "Iraq, crooked as hell. How about bringing baskets of money? Millions and millions of dollars and handing it out? I want to know, who were the soldiers who had that job? Because I think they're living very well right now." Trump offered no proof that this took place. The claim is one of many conspiracy theories he has put forward. In fact, the soldiers who returned home from Iraq are not doing well. They served their country in a war without a clear objective, and on their return found that the Republicans who sent them there had no interest in helping them.
